title: Seattle Seahawks Put Starting Guard
body:
Seattle’s offensive line suffered a significant blow on Wednesday when starting right guard Anthony Bradford was placed on injured reserve, sidelining him for a minimum of four games. The move forces head coach Pete Carroll to reshuffle the interior line and could have ripple effects on the Seahawks’ rushing attack and pass‑protection schemes as the team pushes through a challenging mid‑season stretch.

Bradford, a second‑round pick in 2022, entered the season as the Seahawks’ projected starter at right guard and quickly earned a reputation for his blend of athleticism and technique. He has been a key component in the unit’s ability to open lanes for running back Kenneth Walker III and to keep quarterback Geno Smith upright against increasingly sophisticated defensive fronts. The injury, which was reportedly sustained during practice earlier in the week, is expected to keep him out through at least Week 9, though the exact timeline will depend on the nature of the damage and the team’s medical assessment.

In response to the loss, the Seahawks have elevated safety Rodney Cameron to the active roster, a maneuver that underscores the depth challenges the club faces on the offensive line. Cameron, who has primarily contributed on special teams and as a backup safety, will likely see his first significant action on the line of scrimmage. The move signals that Seattle may have to rely on a combination of utility players and perhaps a fresh look at the practice squad to fill the void. Veteran guard Luke Watson, who has been a reliable swing‑guard throughout his career, is expected to see increased snaps, while younger prospects such as Ethan Miller may receive a chance to prove themselves in a regular‑season setting.

The timing of Bradford’s injury could not be more consequential. Seattle sits at a crossroads in the NFC West, trailing the division leader by a narrow margin and needing to secure wins against both conference rivals and formidable non‑division opponents. The Seahawks have leaned heavily on their ground game to control tempo, averaging 4.6 yards per carry over the first six weeks. Without Bradford’s blocking prowess, the effectiveness of that strategy may be tested. Defensive coordinators around the league have already noted Seattle’s interior line as a potential weakness; a diminished line could translate into increased pressure on Smith, who has already faced a 3.5 sack rate per game.

Analysts also point to the broader implications for Seattle’s roster construction. The team entered the offseason with a modest allocation of cap space for interior linemen, opting instead to invest in skill positions and defensive playmakers. Bradford’s injury highlights the risk of that approach, as depth at guard has historically been a challenge for the franchise. General manager John L. Peters will likely be forced to consider short‑term solutions, such as signing a veteran free agent or promoting a practice‑squad lineman, while also weighing the long‑term impact on the team’s salary‑cap flexibility.

Looking ahead, the Seahawks’ next four games will serve as a litmus test for the unit’s adaptability. If the coaching staff can successfully integrate Cameron and other backups without a steep drop in offensive efficiency, Seattle may mitigate the setback and maintain its playoff push. Conversely, prolonged struggles in the trenches could expose the team’s vulnerability and provide an opening for division rivals to pull ahead. As the season progresses, all eyes will be on how quickly the Seahawks can adjust to Bradford’s absence and whether the depth they have cultivated can sustain a competitive edge in a tightly contested NFC West.
